newsitem.title: UK: Bond funds shy from EMU convergence trades.
newsitem.headline: Bond funds shy from EMU convergence trades.

text.p: Bond fund managers are concentrating on their core holdings and turning away from convergence trades in European bonds in the run up towards a single European currency, at least for the moment.

Even last week's widening spreads, or price differentials, failed to tempt them back into peripheral European bond markets like Italy and Spain, despite a widely held view that the single currency will go ahead on time.

"We believe a lot of EMU momentum and optimism has already been discounted by the market, which implies concentrating investment in Europe in the core markets," Bas Vliegenthart, director of fixed income at Robeco Group in Rotterdam, said on Tuesday.

"We have neutral positions in Spain and Italy, contrary to the past when we've been overweight. So we're not negative, but we doubt if they can further outperform German and Dutch bonds near term," added Vliegenthart, who manages the Rorento Fund with $3.6 billion in fixed income.
Renewed doubts about a delay to European economic and monetary union (EMU) last week prompted BTP/Bund spreads to billow out by 30 basis points to 195 over the week. It was at 188 at midday.

"For the time being I think that's all noise rather than a fundamental development," said Vliegenthart. "I'm keeping the duration the same with overweight in core. I need more indications that fundamental things are changing in Europe."

Neil Ellerbeck, global fixed income and currency porfolio manager at Chase Asset Management in London, which has around $1.75 billion invested in fixed income assets like bonds, said he had already adjusted his holding of Italian and Spanish bonds in a defensive move.

"While we don't think there will be a blow-up in EMU, an amount of good news has been priced in and our yield curve shape forecast meant it made sense to reduce duration in Italy and Spain to the three to five year area," he said.
Ellerbeck added he had generated cash by selling five-year Italy paper two weeks ago, which he was now looking to reinvest.

"We will treat a market sell-off as a small buying opportunity at some stage, for example if the BTP/Bund spread balloons over 250 basis points in the five year area. This may be a short term buy, but again, not with any heavy exposure."
That spread is currently around 243 basis points.
Fund managers based their short term allocation decisions on the premise that EMU would go ahead in some form.
"Our view is that it is highly probable EMU will come on stream on January 1, 1999, for the simple reason there's a lot of political will to finalise the project," said Vliegenthart.
Ellerbeck agreed that EMU will occur in one form or another, but possibly with a small delay.

"Our longer term view is that convergence will occur and EMU will occur," he said. "But given the degree of convergence we've seen, it makes sense to review the process here. So in the near term we're taking some allocation away from the convergence market and putting it into cash."
Miguel Arraya, director of fixed income at Matheson Securities Channel Islands Ltd, said he had also been paring back allocations to peripheral currencies.
"We're focused on tier one countries like Holland, Germany and France and tier two countries like Ireland and Denmark, then sterling as an EMU hedge," he said.
"We took profits on the lira as we took the view that it was unlikely Italy will be in by 1999 -- it's unlikely the Germans want them in," Arraya added.
Analysts expected spread volatility to continue.
"There's going to be some number hopping on economic data and political noise," said Ellerbeck.
Vliegenthart said some doubts would emerge as the critical date for EMU draws near. "But for now, I have no indication that fundamentally things have changed," he said.
